paper_title: Accord: Universal Online Metric Localization and Dense Mapping from one Camera and an IMU

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Dense metric mapping from a single camera and IMU remains challenging: visual-inertial odometry (VIO) provides metric motion but sparse geometry, whereas feed-forward depth models predict dense structure without ensuring metric scale. We present Accord, which constructs an accurate online dense metric map from any camera with an IMU. A VIO filter publishes metric poses, a depth foundation model conditioned on them predicts depth for short keyframe windows, and a factor graph fuses the resulting submaps. Recent work has explored several approaches to this problem. What is essential is the multi-view agreement (Accord), which is considered in SLAM as a source of geometric self-consistency. Accord anchors each keyframe window to metric 3D points triangulated from the filter poses, then exploits bidirectional dense depth agreement between co-visible images to estimate and correct per-image scale errors while preserving the metric scale established by the anchors. Context keyframes further improve depth prediction, and the resulting submaps are fused in a factor graph. We evaluate a single mapping configuration across five public camera-IMU setups and a new Phone-rig/GoPro dataset. With nothing tuned per dataset/setup and every map aligned only by Accord's own trajectory, Accord achieves consistently best/second-best mean F-score at 5 cm on every platform. Accord is open-source along with the phone-rig dataset for the benefit of the research community

Introduction robot that moves and acts autonomously plans in dense, metric map of the space its camera moves through. Yet dense metric mapping and localization still rely on depth cameras, LiDAR, or specific custom sensor rigs, even though nearly every handheld device (smartphones included) already 1 carries camera and an inertial measurement unit (IMU). Two lines of works each recover part of what is needed from these sensors. Visualinertial odometry (VIO) estimates metric motion in real-time [3, 5, 20, 23], but its map consists of only few hundred sparse landmarks. On the other hand, feed-forward geometry models [8, 13, 14, 3032] predict dense structure from uncalibrated images in single forward pass, but not its metric scale and have no sense of gravity direction. SLAM systems built on them align their submaps only up to similarity or projective transformation [17, 21], and are evaluated against the reference only after such an alignment. The two are complementary, and recent work combines learned regressed geometry with visualinertial estimation [19, 24, 26, 38, 39, 41]. We build on DAVIO [19], which conditions depth foundation model, Depth Anything 3 (DA3) [14], on the poses of VIO filter, and address the remaining challenge of metric scale consistency. Although the poses are metric, the predicted depths retain imagedependent scale errors that accumulate across keyframe windows and cannot be revealed by their internal geometric consistency. In practice, these errors can reach few percent: at depth of three meters, two-percent scale error amounts to six centimeters, already exceeding the five-centimeter tolerance used in our evaluation that uses F-Score at 5 cm. Such errors are hidden when maps are evaluated after similarity alignment, but remain visible when placed using their own trajectories. We therefore aim to make the scale of every image metric and mutually consistent, and evaluate maps without fitting their scale to the reference as parts, but as whole map including error from drifting. We introduce Accord, an online dense mapping system that addresses this problem at two levels. First, each keyframe window is anchored to metric 3D points triangulated using the filters poses. These points are obtained from relative poses shared by the keyframes. Consequently, pose errors can shift them, making them mutually consistent while jointly biased. Each image can therefore retain common scale error that cannot be detected from its own triangulated keypoints. The missing constraint comes from the map itself. We exploit bidirectional dense depth agreement between images from different windows observing the same surfaces to estimate and correct per-image scale errors. The agreement measures the difference between the scale errors of two images, while its sensitivity to pose errors depends on scene depth rather than the shorter triangulation baseline. From all such pairs, we solve one correction per image without labels, preserving the overall scale established by the metric anchors (Sec. 4.1). The correction requires no training or ground-truth depth and runs asynchronously without delaying mapping. The mapper never waits for the correction process and incorporates its latest available estimates, allowing the live map to remain scale-corrected. We further introduce context keyframes to improve the geometric predictions of the depth model. Accord is intended to be universal solution that can be used on different everyday use devices, such as smartphones, to provide metric dense mapping. The mapper and depth model use single configuration across different platforms. Each platform provides its rig file, including camera calibration, the camera-to-IMU transformation, and IMU noise parameters, as required by any VIO estimator. We evaluate Accord with single mapping configuration across five public cameraIMU setups and new smartphone/GoPro dataset. Accord achieves the best mean map F-score among the evaluated dense pipelines on every public dataset with scan. On our smartphone/GoPro dataset, it achieves the best or second best mean score. Contributions. Scale-consistent mapping on pose-conditioned depth model: metric anchor per window from keypoints on filtered depth; label-free correction per image, measured by the dense multi-view two-way agreement of images that see one surface and solved online off the mapping path; and context keyframes for the depth model (Sec. 4). One configuration across platforms, scored at the maps own placement: five public setups, against five other dense pipelines and two VIO sparse systems. Plus additional everyday-use devices (smartphones, GoPro) to ensure consistent robust dense metric mapping for general use cases. (Sec. 5). smartphone rig dataset: eleven campus walks by day and at night from two phones carried together, with LiDAR phones map as the reference (Sec. 5.2), to be released. 2. Related Work Feed-forward geometry and SLAM. DUSt3R [31] and MASt3R [13] predict pairwise point maps, while VGGT [30] and π3 [32] jointly predict geometry and camera poses from multiple images. MapAnything [8] and DA3 [14] also support reconstruction conditioned on supplied camera intrinsics and poses. Building on feed-forward predictions, SLAM systems align geometry through Sim(3) or SL(4) optimization [6, 12, 17, 18, 21]. Joint pose and depth optimization is another central component of learned SLAM, as exemplified by DROID-SLAM [29] and, more recently, FoundationSLAM [34], which incorporates depth foundation model. We focus on inter-window depth-scale consistency in poseconditioned mapping while retaining the metric trajectory supplied by visualinertial estimator. Dense visualinertial mapping with learned depth. Learned depth has been used within VIO for dense geometry estimation [42] and initialization [39, 40]. Kimera [25] adds 2 dense mapping to visualinertial estimation, SimpleMapping [35] uses VIO poses and sparse points to guide learned multi-view stereo, and OKVIS2-X [1, 7] couples uncertaintyaware dense mapping with state estimation. MASt3RFusion [41] integrates feed-forward visual alignment with IMU and GNSS factors. VIDAR [26] anchors learned mapping to VIO, while ScaRF-SLAM [38] conditions DA3 on tracking poses and optimizes frame and submap scales. FoundationVIO [24] incorporates relative poses predicted by geometric foundation model into an inertial factor graph, jointly estimating camera poses and scale for each image batch. Our method instead builds on the pose-conditioned mapping of DAVIO [19], retaining the filters pose stream while adding metric depth anchoring and inter-frame scale correction. Metric anchoring and scale consistency. VI-Depth [33] aligns monocular depth predictions to sparse visualinertial depth through scale and shift, while visualinertial rescaling has also been used for autonomous aerial navigation [36]. VI3 [15] uses inertial cues to ground pretrained geometry, and Scalix [11] incorporates learned scale uncertainty into monocular SLAM. Beyond metric anchoring, consistency across predictions is addressed through submap alignment [17, 18], frame and submap scale optimization in ScaRF-SLAM [38], temporal consistency in video depth [9, 16], and bidirectional geometric constraints in FoundationSLAM [34]. Following the sparse-to-dense alignment principle, we estimate robust window-level log-scale offset from triangulated metric points. We then use bidirectional dense log-depth comparisons across windows to correct residual per-image scale differences, holding camera poses fixed during this correction. The log-scale corrections sum to zero within each connected component, so their multiplicative factors have geometric mean one. 3. System Overview. Other pipelines. We compare against five baselines: MASt3R-Fusion [41], feed-forward visualinertial system evaluated with the dense map of its global optimization; VGGT-SLAM 2.0 [17], vision-only method rescaled using the reference scale prior to the same rigid alignment; the mapper of ScaRF-SLAM [38], run with its own depth model, on Accords poses. FoundationVIO [24], concurrent method evaluated with its dense map; DAVIO [19], our base system paired with the same depth model. All baselines are run using their released configurations on the same images. 5.1. Public benchmarks Maps. With single configuration, Accords map has the best mean across all four datasets with ground-truth scans (Tab. 2). Notably, the runner-up is different pipeline in each case: VGGT-SLAM 2.0 on EuRoC, ScaRF-SLAMs mapper on ORI, MASt3R-Fusion on Hilti-Oxford, and FoundationVIO on Oxford Spires. Each baseline excels in specific type of scene, yet none ranks among the top two on second dataset; what sets Accord apart is its consistent generalization across platforms. It also holds per sequence  (Fig. 3)  : Accords map has the highest score on 12 of the 17 scanned sequences and one of the two highest on 16. Every pipeline scores far lower on Hilti-Oxford and Oxford Spires than in the rooms and on ORI; confirming that large-scale heritage and outdoor environments remain challenging for every method, Accord included. Where the maps differ. Figure 4 shows what the scores measure. In the room, Accords walls align closely with the reference scan, whereas MASt3R-Fusion produces duplicated walls and ScaRF-SLAMs mapper scatters noisy surfaces across the room. On ORI ScaRF-SLAMs mapper, supplied with our poses, matches our reconstruction quality; FoundationVIO leaves part of the building unmapped, and VGGT-SLAM 2.0s map fractures along the trajectory. Outdoors  (Fig. 5)  , FoundationVIO maps the ground along its path, where its depth is kept, while Accord reaches the facades across the quad. Concurrent work. ScaRF-SLAM [38] and FoundationVIO [24] evaluate maps under local alignment protocol: the path is cut into 10 pieces and each piece is registered to the scan before it is scored, which masks accumulated drift. In contrast, our protocol aligns the entire map once using the systems own trajectory, ensuring that drift is directly reflected as map error. From drone flying indoors to multi-camera rig carried across college quads, Accord achieves the highest mean reconstruction score among all evaluated dense pipelines on every benchmark with ground-truth scans. Both settings were chosen on the development sequences, with the filter alone, by rules written before the runs. The IMUs noise. With the noise of the datasets first configuration, five times the sensors data sheet, the filters scale was too long by up to 14 % on the development sequences. That held in 22 of 23 stands of the development sequences. In the other, on exp07, the camera stands before blank wall at close range, the landmarks leave the state within frame, and the filter, on the IMU alone, drifts 0.57 and jumps 0.22 when the walk resumes.
